claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure containing multiscale domains such as differing grain sizes, phase distributions, and interphase boundaries.
High-throughput quantitative microstructural imaging can provide detailed microstructure data for input into a machine-learning-enhanced multiscale simulation.
An imaging-informed machine-learning framework can refine multiscale mechanical-property simulations of HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical domains such as grain boundaries and phase interfaces influence local stress concentrations in HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical domains influence crack initiation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Detailed imaging data can capture the microstructural features governing local stress concentration and crack initiation.
Multiscale characterization allows the integrated simulation to adjust local stiffness and toughness parameters in real time.
Representing microstructural inhomogeneities produces more physically realistic predictions of macroscopic mechanical response.
The imaging-informed machine-learning simulation will predict tensile Young's modulus more accurately than conventional simulation methods.
The imaging-informed machine-learning simulation will predict yield strength more accurately than conventional simulation methods.
The imaging-informed machine-learning simulation will predict fracture behavior more accurately than conventional simulation methods.
The proposed method will reduce average prediction error for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related parameters by at least 20% relative to conventional simulations.
The proposed method will reduce overall simulation time by approximately 50% relative to conventional simulations.
The conventional comparator uses homogenized material parameters and standard continuum approximations without high-resolution microstructural inputs.
Substantial alteration of the hierarchical microstructure by thermal aging or unexpected phase transformations may cause the approach to fail.
Insufficient imaging resolution may prevent capture of critical features and cause the approach to fail.
The method's effectiveness depends on the quality and representativeness of the microstructural imaging data.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% prediction-error reduction or approximately a 50% computation-time reduction relative to the conventional comparator is declared falsifying.
